sentences.text: The average length of Apatosaurus was 21 to 23 meters with an average mass of 16.4 to 22.4 tonnes.
Most size estimates for Apatosaurus are based on specimen CM 3018, which measures 21 to 23 meters in length and weighs 16.4 to 22.4 tonnes.
Apatosaurus was a large quadruped with a long neck and a long whip-like tail.
Some Apatosaurus specimens indicate a maximum length up to 30% greater than average and a mass between 32.7 and 72.6 tonnes.
A 2015 volumetric study estimated the type specimen CM 3018 weighed between 21.8 and 38.2 tonnes, a mass similar to the Argentine titanosaur Dreadnoughtus.
Giant specimens found in Oklahoma, such as OMNH 1670, were approximately 11–30% longer than the type specimen, suggesting a mass possibly double that of CM 3018, between 33 and 73 tonnes.
Computer modeling suggests Apatosaurus tails could produce cracking sounds over 200 decibels.
The genus Apatosaurus was described by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
The first Apatosaurus fossils were discovered in spring 1877 by miner Arthur Lakes and his friend Henry C. Beckwith in Morrison, Colorado.
Elmer Riggs described a well-preserved diplodocid skeleton from the Grand River Valley near Fruita, Colorado, in 1903.
The Yale Peabody Museum sculpted an Apatosaurus skull based on a Camarasaurus lower jaw and an 1891 illustration by Marsh.
The first Apatosaurus skull was identified in 1975, decades after the genus was named.
Modern research indicates that Apatosaurus was a fully terrestrial animal, contrary to older theories that it lived partly submerged in water.
Studies of its skull suggest Apatosaurus was a ground-height, nonselective browser.
Trackways indicate Apatosaurus could travel up to 40 km per day and potentially reach speeds of 20 to 30 km per hour.
Calculations suggest Apatosaurus's tidal volume would be 904 liters if it had an avian respiratory system, 225 liters if mammalian, or 19 liters if reptilian.
An avian respiratory system would require a lung volume of about 600 liters, which fits within the estimated thoracic space, whereas a mammalian system would require 2,950 liters.
A 1999 study concluded that Apatosaurus grew rapidly as a juvenile and reached near-adult size in about 10 years.
Juvenile Apatosaurus likely had proportionally shorter necks and tails and greater disparity between forelimbs and hindlimbs compared to adults.
Apatosaurus ajax fossils are exclusively found in the upper Brushy Basin Member, dating to 152–151 million years ago.
Researchers suggest Apatosaurus may have swallowed stones called gastrolits to help digest tough plant fibers because its jaws alone were insufficient for chewing.
Most modern paleontologists agree that Apatosaurus and Brontosaurus belong to the same genus, with Apatosaurus having priority as the name.
Many Apatosaurus species were originally named by Marsh based on fragmentary and indistinguishable remains.
Apatosaurus grandis was named by Marsh in 1877 in the same article that described Apatosaurus ajax.
Specimens of Apatosaurus ajax date from the late Kimmeridgian to the early Tithonian ages.
Paleontologist Robert T. Bakker argued in the 1990s that Apatosaurus excelsus should be classified as a separate genus distinct from Apatosaurus ajax.
A 2015 study concluded that Brontosaurus is a distinct genus from Apatosaurus, though this classification is not universally accepted.
A 2012 study by Taylor and Wedel found the material of Apatosaurus minimus difficult to place within Diplodocoidea or Macronaria.
Apatosaurus species have a wider and presumably stronger neck compared to Brontosaurus excelsus.
Apatosaurus lived approximately 152 to 151 million years ago during the Late Jurassic period.
Before the 1970s, scientists theorized that Apatosaurus lived in partially submerged swamps because they were thought to be too massive to support their weight on solid ground.
Recent findings suggest that Apatosaurus was a fully terrestrial animal rather than one that lived in water.
Allosaurus accounted for 70–75% of theropod specimens and was at the top of the Morrison food web.
In 2008, Thomas Lehman and Holly Woodward estimated that an Apatosaurus could grow to 25 tons in 15 years, with a maximum growth of 5 tons in a single year.
